## Results

Initial XRD check
A room-temperature lab XRD was first performed to quickly check the crystal structure of the as-synthesized PZO. Figure 1 shows the pattern that can be well indexed into the fcc structure with a lattice parameter of 5.43 Å. Therefore, PZO can also be viewed as a fluorite structured composition of Pr0.75Zr0.25O2 after doping ZrO2 into PrO2 in a stoichiometric ratio of Pr:Zr = 3:1.

VTND analysis
To precisely examine the evolutions of crystal structure and crystallographic parameters of PZO with temperature and atmospheres, we employed VTND (Variable Temperature Neutron Diffraction). The VTND patterns in 2D and 3D contour style collected in the range of RT-900 °C in argon (relevant to TC condition) are shown in Fig. 2a, b. The real-time phase evolution can be clearly visualized from the intensity contour plots. The refined crystal structure is shown in Fig. 2c along with refinement data listed in Table S1 of the Supplementary Information (SI).

At room temperature, the diffraction patterns can be well refined into space group Fm3¯m (No. 225) with very low Bragg-intensity R values (Rp) and weight-profile R value (Rwp). In this fluorite structure, Pr/Zr and O occupies (0, 0, 0) and (1/4, 1/4, 1/4), respectively. More importantly, Zr shares Pr position with 25% occupancy without showing a long-range ordering, which suggests that the original Pr3ZrO8-δ can be viewed as Pr0.75Zr0.25O2-δ. It is also interesting to note that 91.5% of the O-site in PZO is occupied at RT, suggesting 8.5% oxygen vacancies (δo=0.17) and the as-synthesized PZO composition as Pr0.75Zr0.25O1.83 at RT.

With the same fcc structure, we also refined VTND patterns at other temperatures. The original refined patterns and refined structure are provided in Fig. S1 with data in Table S1. From these data, we can conclude that PZO retains its fcc structure from RT to 900 °C in argon with neither phase transition nor impurity detected, indicating thermal stability of PZO in argon up to 900 °C. Similar datasets collected in air and refinement performed are provided in Figs. S2–S3 and Table S2. As evident from these results, there is no phase change from RT to 900 °C in air either.

The refined lattice parameter, unit cell volume and bond length between Pr(Zr) and O as a function of T in air and argon are compared in Fig. 3. In air, lattice parameter a (Å), unit cell volume (Å3) and Pr(Zr)-O bond length (Å) increase with T as expected. In argon, a similar trend with T is observed. However, the lattice parameter, unit volume and Pr(Zr)-O bond length of PZO are all larger in argon than in air. These increases are obviously caused by the loss of lattice oxygen that weakens Pr(Zr)-O interactions and formation of large Pr3+28,29, allowing lattice to expand and Pr-O bond to elongate.

It is interesting to point out that the lattice parameter measured in air exhibits a small contraction with time at 300 °C, signaling that there might be a small change in lattice oxygen content. In comparison, the lattice parameter measured at 300 °C in argon exhibits a significant increase in the later stage of the 300 °C-holding period, further inferring a possible change in lattice oxygen content. Our later TGA and TC cycling results suggest that this is likely related to the dynamics of oxygen release. While the lattice parameter measured in air remains normal at higher temperatures, they exhibit slightly different behaviors in argon. The first is from 400 to 500 °C, where there is a significant change in lattice parameter, followed by a slower change from 500 to 600 °C. Another occurs at 800 °C, where the expected plateau is taken over by a slower increase. Again, these lattice parameter abnormalities signal that there are some subtle changes in the PZO’s lattice oxygen content (and Pr oxidation state) with T, particularly in atmospheres with low pO2, although there is no clear evidence of phase transformation from all VTND patterns shown. With the data available, we hypothesize that Fig. 3a is the result of change in oxygen stoichiometry accompanied by the corresponding change in Pr-oxidation state and elongation of Pr-O bond. Oxygen occupancy cannot be precisely determined to further understand these subtle changes due to the short-time-bin data collection during the T-ramping period.

Phase stability of fcc-PZO
The phase stability of fcc-PZO under the working conditions of TC processes is critically important to the stability of H2/O2 yields. To determine the phase stability, we exposed the as-synthesized fcc-PZO samples in different T and pO2, followed by quenching the samples from high temperatures and analyzing the phase composition by XRD. According to the identified phases, we construct the phase stability diagram in Fig. 4. The original XRD patterns can be found in Fig. S4 in the SI. The impurities identified are Pr3+ compounds: Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7. A general trend is that the higher the pO2, the higher the T that fcc-PZO is stable.

We also performed high-temperature XRD (HTXRD) in air (pO2 = 0.21 atm) and high vacuum (pO2 ~ 10−9 atm) from RT to 1100 °C as an independent verification. The original HTXRD patterns are shown in Fig. S5. Shown in diamond in Fig. 4 are the phases identified by HTXRD; they fall well within the phase regions constructed from ex-situ XRD data, indicating the accuracy of the phase diagram.

We also attempted to construct the phase stability diagram using hybrid DFT coupling spin-orbital interactions; the details about the approach are provided in the Experimental section. Figure S6 shows the calculated phase stability diagram of the PZO system using this method. With the consideration of temperature and configurational entropy, the calculations show that a stable PZO phase could be formed.

Oxygen off-stoichiometry vs. T and pO2
Oxygen off-stoichiometry (δ) is a key parameter determining the performance of RAO in TC cycles. A precise determination of δ as a function of T and pO2 is critically important to understand the performance of PZO for TC applications. Therefore, we selected both VTND and TGA methods to evaluate δ of PZO. The VTND-derived δ values were taken as the twice the fraction of the unoccupied O-sites obtained from refinement; Tables S1 and S2 list these values measured in both air and argon and air, respectively. At RT, δo = 0.17, which is the same as δo = 0.17 estimated by XPS and XAS based on the oxidation state of Pr; see Figs. S7 and S8 in the SI.

To confirm the VTND-derived δ, we also performed TGA measurements; the original weight loss curves are shown in Fig. S9, from which δ = δ(T) is derived using δo = 0.17 as the starting value. Figure 5a compares the two sets of δ in the formula of Pr0.75Zr0.25O2-δ. Note that VTND-data are only available in air and argon. The VTND-derived δ consistently exhibits a slightly higher value than its TGA-derived counterpart in both atmospheres. Within the experimental error, the two sets of δ-values agree with each other. Correspondingly, the oxidation state of Pr is also plotted against T in the second y-axis in Fig. 5a. As is shown, the average oxidation state of Pr decreases as T increases and pO2 decreases, implying that more Pr3+ is formed while the lattice oxygen is being lost. A plot of log δ vs. 1/T shown in Fig. 5b confirms that the loss of oxygen or the formation of oxygen vacancies is a thermally activated process following Arrhenius relationship with a very low activation energy of 0.02−0.03 eV, suggesting that the thermal oxygen release in PZO is a very facile process. An early study has also confirmed in CeO2-ZrO2 system that Zr4+ facilitates reducibility of pure CeO230. Our DFT calculations also confirm the low formation energy of oxygen vacancies in fcc-PZO even at oxygen-rich condition, see Figs. S10–S11 in the SI; details about the DFT method are provided in the Experimental Methods section.

A simple conversion of Pr-oxidation state shown in Fig. 5a into Pr3+ concentration ([Pr3+]) using charge neutrality indicates that there is ~75% Pr3+ present in the fcc-PZO under 900 oC and N2, see Fig. S12, which is in striking difference from pure PrO2; the latter turns into Pr2O3 or other lower oxidation state intermediates (PrnO2n-2) under this condition31. Therefore, it is reasonable to believe that Zr4+ stabilizes Pr4+, likely due to its fixed-valence substitution.

To compare with the benchmark CeO2-δ, we further plot δ-pO2-T of fcc-PZO in Fig. 6. A first glance indicates that fcc-PZO exhibits much higher δ than CeO2-δ, particularly at lower T range. To put this into perspective, δ at 900 °C in argon and in air are 0.27 and 0.24, respectively. For the benchmark CeO2-δ, it is in the order of 10−4 and 10−3 in air and argon, respectively19,32. The significant advantage of PZO in δre over CeO2-δ strongly suggests that PZO is a promising RAO for intermediate temperature TC processes.

Understanding electrical conductivity vs. T and pO2
Electrical conductivity is a crucial indicator of bulk diffusion of ions/electrons and charge transfer kinetics at the surface of PZO. The measured total electrical conductivity σ of PZO as a function of pO2 and T is shown in Fig. 7. The level of conductivity over the entire pO2 and T ranges studied is rather low (10−2 to 10−3 S/cm) but comparable to CeO2-δ at much higher temperatures and lower pO2. Collectively, Fig. 7 indicates that PZO is a semiconductor with a low activation energy Ea = 0.34−0.43 eV (Fig. 7b). At high pO2 range (>10-4 atm), Fig. 7a indicates that fcc-PZO displays a p-type conducting behavior. As pO2 decreases, σ first experiences a plateau, an indicative of dominance of ionic defects, then a weak n-type conducting behavior.

To interpret the conductivity behavior described above, we developed a simplified defect-chemistry model based on the “dilute solution” approximation; full derivations are provided in the Supplementary Information. Briefly, the model adopts the fluorite (fcc) lattice as the reference framework and assumes Pr4+ (Pr×Pr) as the base oxidation state. Under a given T and pO2, oxygen loss generates oxygen vacancy (V••O), Pr3+ (Pr'Pr) species as described by reaction (S1) in the SI.

At high pO2 (>10−3 atm), oxygen vacancies are oxidized to produce electron holes (reaction (S2)), giving rise to p-type conductivity. Conversely, at low pO2 (<10−7 atm), lattice oxygen (O×O) is removed (reaction (S3)), generating free electrons and yielding n-type conductivity. In the intermediate pO2 range (~10−7 to 10−3 atm), ionic defects (V••O and Pr'Pr) dominate, while electronic carriers remain minority species. Consequently, overall conductivity becomes less sensitive to pO2. We note that both oxygen vacancies and electrons are present in fcc-PZO at comparatively high concentrations; however, because electrons possess much higher mobility, the total conductivity is still dominated by electronic charge transport even within the intermediate pO2 regime. Therefore, fcc-PZO is deemed a mixed electronic and oxide-ion conductor.

The above defect-chemistry picture is consistent with prior band-structure studies on Pr oxides. These studies show that the partially filled Pr4+ 4f1 band resides near the Fermi level and strongly hybridizes with the O-2p valance band, leading PrO2-δ, including fcc-PZO, to exhibit narrow-band semiconducting behavior with a band gap ~0.5 eV associated with mixed Pr3+/Pr4+ valance state33. This prediction agrees with the measured activation energy of ~0.4 eV in Fig. 7b. In contrast, Pr3+ contains strongly localized 4f2 electrons, and Pr2O3 behaves as a Mott insulator with a significantly large band gap (3.5–4.5 eV) between the O-2p valance band and Pr-5d/4f conduction band34. Because Pr4+ species provide the electronic states that facilitate charge transport, the conductivity naturally decreases as the Pr4+ concentration diminishes with decreasing pO2. Notably, a substantial amount of Pr4+ - approximately 25% even under 900 oC and N2 condition - is observed in the fcc-PZO system (Fig. S12).

Thermochemical performance of PZO
To search for the best TC working conditions, we first performed single-cycle testing on fcc-PZO under different T-window (i.e., between Ttr and Tws) and H2O contents. Note that the high T-value within the T-window represents the temperature (Ttr) for thermal reduction cycle, whereas the low T-value is the temperature (Tws) for water splitting reaction cycle. Figure 8a shows the effect of T-window on H2 generation flux under a fixed 20% H2O-Ar; the corresponding set of O2 flux is given in Fig. S14a. It is evident that there is a significant gain in H2 flux from 1100 to 900 °C window to 1100–500 °C window, but no significant gain is observed for 1100–400 °C window. On the other hand, cycling within 900–400 °C produces similar H2 flux as 1100–900 °C cycling. However, our phase diagram (Fig. 4) as well as the following post-test analysis indicate that exposure of fcc-PZO to argon above 1000 °C leads to its decomposition to Pr2O3. Therefore, 900–400 °C is selected as the T-window for TC cycling of fcc-PZO. On the other hand, the effect of H2O on H2 flux is shown in Fig. 8b along with the corresponding O2 flux shown in Fig. S14b, suggesting that H2O contents higher than 20% do not increase H2 flux significantly within the 400–900 °C window.

These selection of the above cycling conditions, i.e., 900–400 °C and 20% H2O is further supported by the post-test analysis. Figure 8c shows that at Ttr ≥ 1000 °C, fcc-PZO partially decomposes into Pr2O3, which is an oxide-ion and electron insulator and detrimental to TC performance. Upon exposure to 20% H2O for 4 h at 400 °C in the following oxidation cycle, Fig. 8d shows that the fcc-PZO exposed to Ar at Ttr ≤ 900 °C remains unchanged in phase compositions (red patterns). In contrast, for fcc-PZO exposed to 1000 °C in Ar (blue patterns), it is interesting to observe that the Pr2O3 secondary phase is reversed to the original fcc phase after H2O oxidation cycle, demonstrating the reversibility. A partial conversion of Pr2O3 impurity to Pr6O11 is also observed after H2O oxidation of fcc-PZO that was exposed to 1100 °C in argon (green patterns). These results suggest that the reoxidation of Pr2O3 into Pr6O11 or fcc-PZO is thermodynamically feasible but could be kinetically limited. Based on the above results, we, therefore, select 900 °C for thermal reduction cycles in argon and 400 °C for water splitting cycles in 20% H2O.

The original profiles of T, O2 and H2 concentrations collected under this condition over 10 consecutive TC cycles are shown in Fig. 9a, by which the O2/H2 fluxes are converted and plotted against cycle number in Fig. 9b. In general, this level of intermediate-temperature performance is better than most reported in the literature even under higher temperatures, see Table S3 for comparison, demonstrating the potential of fcc-PZO for reduced temperature TC applications. Note that fcc-PZO represents a fundamentally distinct material class from the extensively studied CeO2-ZrO2 solid solution systems; the latter has consistently underperformed the benchmark CeO2-δ 10,19,35–38. Unlike CeO2-ZrO2 solid solutions, fcc-PZO functions more like a compound, akin to CeO2. However, excessive reduction of Pr4+ to Pr3+ could lead to the undesirable formation of Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7, see phase diagram Fig. 4. A key role of Zr in the system is stabilization of the Pr4+/Pr3+ redox couple within the fcc structure by limiting excessive oxygen release, thereby alleviating the formation of the unwanted Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7 impurity phases. Compared to another similar system Ce0.8Pr0.2O2-δ (CPO, the “sweet-spot” composition in the CeO2-Pr2O3 series), where Pr3+ substitution is employed to stabilize oxygen vacancies and lower the reduction enthalpy39–42, fcc-PZO has a clear advantage in δ. For example, the Pr-rich fcc-PZO exhibits δ = 0.20–0.25 in air over 600–900 °C, vs. 0.02–0.08 for CPO39, largely due to suppressed Pr4+ to Pr3+ reduction by Zr4+.

It is evident from Fig. 9b that there is more O2 than H2 produced in each cycle, i.e., 331.7 µmol/g for O2 flux vs. 70.3 µmol/g for H2 flux (averaged from the 10 cycles), which significantly deviates from the theoretical ratio of H2/O2 = 2/1. The slow kinetics for water splitting reaction at lower temperature as evidenced by the longer cycle time than thermal reduction cycle, i.e., 2 h vs. 1 h, is likely the reason. In other words, it may take a much longer time for the water splitting cycle to occupy all available oxygen vacancies and reach the theoretical H2 flux. Accumulation of unfilled oxygen vacancies due to incomplete oxidation cycle could lead to a gradual loss of oxygen and hydrogen fluxes during the subsequent reduction cycle, resulting in the degradation shown in Fig. 9b.

It is worth noting that the steam utilization in this laboratory testing is very low, which leads to very low H2/H2O ratio during the water splitting cycle. One concern is whether fcc-PZO is still stable at lower pO2 (higher H2/H2O ratio). To test this possibility, we performed a separate study in which we directly expose fcc-PZO to 4% H2-Ar for 2 h at 900 °C. The XRD pattern of the tested sample is shown in Fig. S15, where the original fcc-PZO peaks remain without any detectable impurity phases. The XRD peaks are slightly shifted to the left, implying increased oxygen off-stoichiometry. Therefore, this study at least confirms that fcc-PZO is stable at 900 °C up to 4% H2.

To facilitate the understanding of the observed degradation, we also examined the morphology of the tested fcc-PZO by SEM and compared it with the one before testing in Fig. S16. No significant change in fcc-PZO morphology can be detected after cycling, which is not surprising given the low temperature operation. Therefore, the degradation is likely due to the slow water splitting kinetics that causes the chain-reaction reducing the amount of available oxygen vacancies to sustain the thermochemical cycling.

Understanding the rate limiting step of the steam splitting cycle
To facilitate the understanding of the underlying reasons for the lower-than-anticipated H2 production in the water splitting cycle and identification of the rate limiting step (RLS), we conducted an analysis of the Gibbs free energy associated with the elementary steps using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. We first constructed three low index surfaces of fcc-PZO, namely, PZO (100), PZO (110), and PZO (111) from the optimized structure of the PZO bulk, as illustrated in Fig. S17. In accordance with the definition of surface energy, the calculated surface energies for PZO (100), PZO (110), and PZO (111) are 2.02, 0.51, and 0.24 J/m2, respectively. Generally, a thermodynamically stable crystal face is characterized by lower surface energy, indicating that the PZO (111) surface is the most stable surface. Consequently, we selected the PZO (111) surface for further DFT analysis. Figure S18 illustrates the construction process of the PZO (111) surface, including the optimized structure of the PZO unit cell, top and side views of the cleaved PZO (111) unit cell, and a 2x1x1 PZO (111) supercell.

The proposed elementary steps occurring on the surface of PZO (111) are as follows: (1) the formation of an oxygen-vacancy site (Ovac); (2) the adsorption of H2O onto an Ovac; (3) the splitting of H2O into two intermediate species (OH*); (4) the breakage of the OH bonds; and (5) the evolution of H2 molecule. Figure 10 illustrates both the top and side views of the reaction pathway along with the structural parameters, as well as the corresponding Gibbs free energy profiles for the H2O splitting process over the PZO (111) surface. Initially, an oxygen vacancy (Ovac) is generated by the release of one lattice oxygen from the pristine PZO (111) surface, which has an oxygen vacancy formation energy of -0.95 eV, see step b. Subsequently, an H2O molecule is adsorbed above the Ovac site, exhibiting an adsorption energy of −0.66 eV, see step c. It is noteworthy from Fig. 10b that, with the formation of the oxygen vacancy and the adsorption of the H2O molecule, the O1 atom in the subsurface gradually moves upward toward the surface. The distances between the O1 atom and the surface for steps a, b, and c are measured at 1.38 Å, 0.63 Å, and 0.10 Å, respectively. As the H atom (labeled as H2) approaches the adjacent O1 atom, a new H2-O1 bond is formed, resulting in its bond length from 1.44 to 1.02 Å. Concurrently, the H2-O3 bond within the H2O molecule breaks, leading to an elongation of its bond length from 1.07 to 1.66 Å. This sequence of events in the dissociation of H2O molecules requires a free energy change of −0.05 eV, forming two isolated OH* intermediates adsorbed on the surface. At step d, the dissociation of the H2O is complete. Subsequently, the two OH bonds, i.e., H2-O1 and H1-O3, are cleaved successively, with the corresponding Gibbs free energies being 0.60 eV and 1.67 eV, respectively. The high energy for H1-O3 cleavage indicates that this step is the RLS toward completing H2 evolution process. The reaction elementary steps and process energies are summarized in Table S4.

We observe that the oxygen vacancy formation energy in Table S4 is negative, implying that a lattice oxygen atom in the PZO (111) surface can be released spontaneously. Consequently, we conducted a further evaluation of the surface’s propensity for oxygen release at higher concentrations of oxygen vacancies. As illustrated in Fig. S19, the formation energies for the first and second oxygen vacancies are −0.95 eV and −0.25 eV, respectively. Moreover, the formation of oxygen vacancies facilitates the migration of subsurface oxygen atoms to the surface. These values indicate that the PZO (111) surface exhibits a strong tendency to release oxygen. Additionally, as illustrated in Fig. 9b, upon the completion of a H2O splitting cycle, we observe that the O1 atom in the subsurface migrates to the surface and forms oxygen molecule with O3, exhibiting an O1-O3 bond length of 1.29 Å. To further evaluate the oxygen release capacity of the PZO (111) surface, we calculated the desorption of this oxygen molecule. The results shown in Fig. S20 indicate a desorption energy of 0.26 eV, again suggesting that the PZO (111) surface can readily release oxygen. Overall, our computational results align well with experimental observations, i.e., the water splitting cycle is the RLS for PZO-based intermediate temperature TC processes, while thermal oxygen release cycle is facile. We are currently working to computationally identify effective surface catalysts that can promote O-H cleavage, followed by testing these catalysts in TC reactor.

In summary, we have demonstrated that PZO crystallizes in a face centered cubic (fcc) structure analogous to CeO2-δ yet exhibits significantly higher oxygen off-stoichiometry (δ), enabling hydrogen generation at lower temperatures. Under thermal reduction in argon at 900 °C, the 10-cycle averaged oxygen flux reaches 331.7 µmol g−1, while hydrogen production achieves 70.3 µmol g−1 at 400 °C with 20% H2O-performance that surpasses both benchmark CeO2-δ and most perovskite oxides under development. A comprehensive investigation combining in situ neutron diffraction, in situ XRD, and ex situ XRD has established the phase stability diagram of the fcc-PZO system, delineating its redox boundaries for thermochemical applications. Supported by experimental validation and hybrid DFT calculations including spin-orbit coupling interactions, a simplified defect chemistry model has been developed that integrates ionic (oxygen vacancies) and electronic (free electrons and holes) defects, providing key insights into charge-carrier transport mechanisms in fcc-PZO.

A remaining challenge for the practical deployment of fcc-PZO in intermediate-temperature TC processes lies in the kinetics of the steam-splitting reaction. Accelerating this step will be critical for realizing the full potential of fcc-PZO. Strategies such as applying surface catalysts or enhancing mixed oxide-ionic and electronic conductivity offer promising pathways to address this limitation. Preliminary DFT calculations indicate that the rate-limiting step (RLS) is the cleavage of the O-H bond on the PZO (111) surface. Overall, this study identifies PZO as a promising redox-active oxide (RAO) for low-temperature thermochemical hydrogen production, operable with a wide range of heat sources.

## Methods

Sample preparation
The Pr3ZrO8-δ (PZO) powder was synthesized by Pechini method. In brief, stoichiometric amounts of high-purity starting materials - Pr(NO₃)₃·6H₂O (97%, Alfa) and ZrO(NO₃)₂·xH₂O (99.97%) - together with citric acid (CA) in a total metal:CA molar ratio of 1:1.5 were dissolved in deionized (DI) water, and a small amount of dilute nitric acid prepared by mixing commercial ~70 wt% HNO₃ with DI water in a 1:9 volume ratio was added to assist dissolution. The solution was then heated at 80 °C to vaporize the solution, followed by heating to 200 °C for autoignition. The resulting powder was first fired at 600 °C for 2 h to fully decompose the precursors into pure oxides. The powder was then dry-pressed into ϕ1″ pellets and sintered at 1050 °C for 10 h in air. To ensure a pure single phase, the sintering step was repeated twice. After sintering, the pellets were ground and ball-milled to obtain a fine powder with an average particle size of ~5.3 μm, which was then loaded into the fixed-bed reactor for thermochemical performance evaluation. The phase composition of the final powder synthesized was pre-checked by a lab powder X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku MiniFlex II) using graphite-monochromatized CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) with a scan rate of 5° min−1 over a 2θ range of 10°–90°. Similarly, the post-cycled PZO was also checked with the lab-scale XRD.

Determination of crystal structure
To precisely determine the crystal structure of PZO and its evolution with temperature, we performed Variable Temperature Neutron Diffraction (VTND) at the VULCAN beamline43 at the Spallation Neutron Source at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The time-of-flight neutron diffraction at 30 Hz chopper setting and high-intensity mode covered a d-space range of 0.45–2.5 Å at the 90° detector bank. To run the VTND experiment, the PZO powders with a particle size of ~5 μm was loaded into a MgO crucible (about 12 mm diameter) to about 20 mm height. The 7 mm × 12 mm opening of neutron incident lights and the 5 mm receiving collimator defined the neutron gauge volume, which was aligned to the sample center to exclude the signals of the crucible and other backgrounds. The sample was moved into a controlled atmosphere furnace for the VTND experiments in both air and argon gas flows44. The diffraction patterns were continuously collected during the heating from the room temperature to 900 °C at a ramp rate of 10 °C/min with 1-h isothermal dwells at 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800 and 900 °C. Specifically, the last 40 min of data of the dwell at each temperature were selected for refinement45.

The Rietveld refinements were conducted using the GSAS program and the EXPGUI46 interface for enhanced usability and convenience45. The background was accurately modeled by employing a shifted Chebyscev function comprising 20 terms in GSAS. To refine the peak profiles, Gaussian width parameters (sig-1 and sig-2) and the Lorentzian width parameter (gam-1) were optimized in a profile function of the back-to-back exponentials with the pseudo-Voigt. Each data set independently underwent refinement for the lattice constant, atomic positions, thermal displacement parameters, and oxygen occupancies (oxygen stoichiometry). Throughout the refinement process, the instrument parameters that dictate the relationship between measured time-of-flight and d-spacing and the absorption correction parameters were consistently maintained across all temperature datasets.

Phase stability determination by XRD
To further elucidate the structural evolution and phase stability of fcc-PZO under different thermal and redox conditions, both ex situ and in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were conducted as a complement to the VTND study.

For ex situ XRD experiments, the as-synthesized fcc-PZO powders were treated under different temperatures ranging from 700 to 1200 °C and pO2 varying from pure O2 to Ar-O2 and 5% H2-Ar mixtures using calibrated mass flow controllers (Alicat). Under each condition, a total of 4-h holding time was given to ensure phase equilibrium. To keep the high temperature phase composition as much as we could, the samples were quenched to RT for XRD analysis. Specifically, after being exposed to a target T and pO2 for 4 h, fcc-PZO samples were rapidly removed from the furnace and immediately quenched in air at room temperature to preserve the high-temperature phase.

We also used in situ XRD to verify the phase diagram constructed from ex situ XRD. The experiments were conducted on an Anton Paar XRK900 reaction chamber under stagnant air and vacuum (~10−9 atm). The samples were heated at a rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ with isothermal holds of 1 h at selected temperatures of 300, 500, 700, 900, and 1100 °C to ensure structural equilibrium at each condition. For each atmosphere, diffraction patterns were continuously acquired during heating and cooling cycles to monitor potential phase transitions and lattice parameter evolution.

All diffraction data were analyzed by Rietveld refinement using the GSAS and EXPGUI suite to extract lattice constants, thermal parameters, and oxygen site occupancies. Consistent refinement protocols were maintained across all datasets to ensure comparability with the VTND results.

Determination of oxygen off-stoichiometry
The oxygen off-stoichiometry (δ) is a critical indicator for the performance of RAO materials. The δ-value at room temperature (denoted as δo) in as-prepared fcc-PZO in air was determined by X-ray photoelectrons spectrometer (XPS), X-ray absorption Spectroscopy (XAS), Thermogravimetry Analysis (TGA) and VTND.

For XPS analysis, a Kratos Axis Ultra DLD instrument equipped with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source (15 kV, 10 mA) was employed. The beam was focused on a 0.7 mm × 0.3 mm area of the sample surface tilted at 45° to the analyzer. The electron energy analyzer was operated at a pass energy of 40 eV for high-resolution scans and 80 eV for survey scans. A step size of 0.05 eV was used, and each peak was scanned twice to ensure signal reliability. The relative proportions of Pr3+ and Pr4+ were determined from deconvoluted Pr 3d spectra, and δo was then calculated based on charge neutrality.

For XAS analysis, the δo in as-prepared fcc-PZO in air was calculated from the averaged Pr oxidation state determined by a lab XAS system (easyXAFS 300+) with energy range of 4.5 to 25 eV calibrated by Cr foil for Pr and Zr foil for Zr, respectively. The measurement mode is transmission and sample aperture is 11 × 3.4 mm. The XAS measurements were performed at Pr L3-edge. The ratio of Pr3+ to Pr4+ obtained from linear combination fitting of reference spectra was used to estimate δo through charge balance. The total measurement time is 1.5 h. During the measurements, three reference materials were used: ZrO2, Pr6O11 and Pr2O3 to ensure the accuracy of the data.

To directly determine δ as a function of temperature (T) and oxygen partial pressure (pO2), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed using a Netzsch STA 448 instrument. The weight change of fcc-PZO was continuously recorded at 300, 500, 700, 900, and 1050 °C under different controlled atmospheres, including ultrahigh-purity Ar, air, 50% O2/Ar, and 100% O2. The δ = δ(T, pO2) values were calculated from the measured weight loss, referenced to the initial δo. The comparison of TGA-derived δ values with those obtained from VTND showed good agreement, validating the combined approach for determining δ of fcc-PZO under variable redox conditions.

Electrical conductivity measurement
Electrical conductivity (σ) is an important indicator to the rates of bulk oxide-ion transport and surface oxygen exchange kinetics. To obtain σ = σ(T, pO2), we use a conventional four-probe technique and measure resistance of a cylindrical sample with a DC method. The cylindrical sample was made by pressing the powder into a dimension of ϕ1/4’’ × 1/2’’ and sintering into a dense body at 1050 °C in air for 10 h. Two pairs of silver paste/mesh were attached to both ends of the cylinder to ensure proper electrical contact for current passage, while another two sets of voltage tabs were adhered to the body of the cylinder with a pre-defined distance. The measurements were carried out from T = 400 to 900 °C and pO2 = 10−14 to 1 atm. The variation of pO2 was achieved by mixing pure O2 with Ar for pO2 ≥ 10-6 atm gases and mixing Ar-10% H2 with Ar and moisture for pO2 ≤ 10−14 atm gases. The final pO2 was determined by a home made tubular oxygen sensor placed next to the sample.

Defect chemistry modeling
The first step in building the model is to determine the base crystal structure of the material, Previous studies have shown that Pr1-xZrxO2-δ system can exhibit both pyrochlore and fluorite structures depending on the Zr content, as well as the presence of both 3+ and 4+ oxidation states for praseodymium47,48. Our XRD and VTND results confirm that Pr0.75Zr0.25O2-δ specifically exhibits fluorite structure which agrees with the finding from the literature47,48. Accordingly, we assume that structure in our model and set Pr4+ as our base oxidation.

The second step is to write the defect reactions to encompass various ionic and electronic point defects. With these reactions, mass action law is applied to express equilibrium constant (K). The defect chemistry modeling section in SI provides details on these defect reactions.

The third step is to solve these defect reaction equilibria. We adopted lsqnonlin function in MATLAB to do so. With the numerical solutions to the defect reaction, we obtain thermodynamic quantities of these defect reactions such as enthalpy (ΔH) and entropy (ΔS) from temperature-dependence of K. We also obtain transport properties such as diffusivities of charge carriers using Nernst-Einstein equation with charge carrier concentrations as the fitting parameters.

TC performance evaluation
A fixed bed flow reactor was employed to characterize the performance of fcc-PZO in TC cycling. Figure S21 shows the schematic of the reactor. A quartz tube with two-diameter (1/2’’ and 1/4’’) sections was used, where ~0.5 g of fcc-PZO powder was loaded in the 1/2’’-section connecting to the gas inlet, whereas the 1/4’’-section was connected to a Mass Spectrometer (MS, Pfeiffer OmniStar® GSD 350) at the outlet to analyze the gas composition. To minimize the potential sintering of fcc-PZO, a flow of 60 mL/min Ar was used to support the powder bed. After the thermochemical cycle, different temperature flows was used with different steam contents for the water splitting cycle. The temperature window for the TC cycling varied between 1100 to 400 °C and the steam contents varied from 3 to 50%. After the test, the phase and morphology of the fcc-PZO samples were examined by XRD and a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Zeiss Ultraplus).

DFT calculations of defect formation energy
The Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP 6.5.1) code49 with the projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials50 was used in density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The cutoff energy for the plane wave expansion is 520 eV. To take into account the Coulomb correlation, we employed the Heyd–Scuseria–Ernzerhof (HSE)51 hybrid functional with 15% exact-exchange mixing and a screening parameter of 0.3 (HSE03)52. This yields a lattice parameter of 5.32 Å and a band gap of 1.73 eV. The former is close to the experimental 5.34 Å, reflecting the adequacy of the lattice constructed. The calculated defect-free bandgap is higher than 2Ea = 0.8-0.9 eV observed from electrical conductivity plot (Fig. 7). Applying a standard temperature (electron-phonon) renormalization yields a band gap ~1.1 ± 0.1 eV at 0 K. With the consideration of disorder/defect effect, the true quasiparticle gap could be higher, getting closer to the measured Ea.

Spin polarization and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) was included throughout all calculations. We adopted a 4×4×4 k-point grid for Brillouin zone (BZ) integration for the Pr3ZrO8 primitive cell. Regarding defect calculations, a larger 2×2 supercell with 96 atoms is built and BZ integration is performed based on a single Γ-point. All atoms are relaxed until the Hellmann-Feynman forces acting on individual atom becomes smaller than 0.01 eV/Å.

The formation energy Ef(Xq) of a defect X in charge state q is defined as53:

Ef(Xq) = Edef(Xq) - Ehost + Σ ni Δμi + q(ΔEF + ϵVBM) + Ecorr (3)

where Edef(Xq) is the total energy derived from a supercell calculation containing the defect X, and Ehost is the total energy for the perfect crystal using an equivalent supercell. The integer ni indicates the number of atoms of type i (here i could be Pr, Zr, or O) that have been added to (ni > 0) or removed from (ni < 0) the supercell. Ei are the total energy per atom of elementary substance of type i species. Δμi corresponds to chemical potentials of these species, referenced to Ei, with Δμi = 0 as the element-rich limit. The analog of the chemical potential for “charge” q is given by the chemical potential of the electrons, i.e., the Fermi energy ΔEF, using the valance band maximum (VBM) of host supercell ϵVBM as reference. Ecorr is charge correction.

Based on defect formation energy, the charge-state transition level ϵ(q1/q2) is defined as the Fermi-level position for which the formation energies of charge states q1 and q2 are equal53–55:

ϵ(q1/q2) = [Ef(Xq1; ΔEF=0) - Ef(Xq2; ΔEF=0)] / (q2 - q1) (4)

where Ef(Xq; ΔEF=0) is the formation energy of the defect X in the charge state q when the Fermi level is at the VBM (ΔEF = 0).

A thermodynamically consistent process for determining the bounds of chemical potentials is outlined below. The total energy of a stoichiometric unit of Pr3ZrO8 can be expressed as:

3μPr + μZr + 8μO = Eb(Pr3ZrO8) - 3Eb(Pr) - Eb(Zr) - 8Eg(O2) = ΔH(Pr3ZrO8) (5)

where ΔH(Pr3ZrO8) is the formation enthalpy of Pr3ZrO8. The stability of the system against decomposition into its constituent elements places upper limits on the chemical potential of each element in Pr3ZrO8. Therefore, additional restrictions are determined by:

μPr ≤ 0
μZr ≤ 0
μO ≤ 0 (6)

To ensure that the binary oxides (PrO2, ZrO2, and Pr2O3) do not precipitate from Pr3ZrO8, the following restrictions are also included:

μPr + 2μO ≤ ΔH(PrO2)
μZr + 2μO ≤ ΔH(ZrO2)
2μPr + 3μO ≤ ΔH(Pr2O3) (7)

where ΔH(PrO2), ΔH(ZrO2), and ΔH(Pr2O3) are the formation enthalpies of PrO2, ZrO2, and Pr2O3.

The above set of equations defines the range of chemical potentials consistent with the stability of Pr3ZrO8 against decomposition into binary oxides or into its elemental components. Given the bounds for the chemical potential of each element, a valid range for the formation energies of specific defects with various charge states can be examined.

DFT understanding of steam splitting process on the surface of fcc-PZO
To understand the reaction mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations using the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP 5.4.1)49,56. In the calculations, the projector augmented wave (PAW)57 method and the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE)58 functional were employed to describe ion-electron interactions and account for electronic exchange and correlation effects, respectively. To ensure the accuracy of the calculations, the energy cut-off for the plane waves was set to 450 eV, and the total energy and forces were set to 10-4 eV and 0.05 eV/Å, respectively. The first Brillouin zone was sampled using a 2×4×1 k-mesh for the PZO (111) supercell generated using the Γ-centered Monkhorst-Pack scheme59. A vacuum region of more than 17 Å was introduced along the z-direction to avoid interactions between periodically repeated images. The valence electron configurations considered were H 1s1, O 2s22p4, Zr 4s24p65s14d3, and Pr 5s25p66s25d1, respectively. Given that the systems include H2O molecular adsorption, the van der Waals (vdW) interactions between the H2O molecule and surface could be significant, thus, the DFT-D3 dispersion correction within the Grimme scheme was applied60. Spin polarization was considered in all calculations. In the present calculations, all atoms were fully relaxed for the unit cell optimization of PZO, while for the calculations of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and H2O-splitting over the PZO (111) surface, the bottom 12 atom layers were fixed to represent the bulk of PZO, with the top 6 atom layers and adsorbate fully relaxed.

The PZO (111) surface was constructed from an optimized 5.43 Å × 5.43 Å × 5.43 Å PZO unit cell, which comprised 3 Pr, 1 Zr, and 8 O atoms, as shown in Fig. S16a. Initially, a 6-arrangement period in the c direction (18-atom layer) clean PZO (111) surface, terminating with Pr, Zr and O atoms, was generated by cleaving from the PZO unit cell, and subsequently expanded into a 2×1×1 supercell, see Fig. S16b, c. The surface formation energy of PZO (Esur) is defined as

Esur = (Eslab - (Nslab/Nbulk)Ebulk) / 2S (8)

where Eslab and Ebulk are the total energy of the slab and PZO bulk, respectively. Nslab and Nbulk are the number of PZO units contained in the slab and bulk, respectively. S is the area of the PZO surface.

The formation energy of oxygen vacancy (Ef) is calculated by

Ef = E(Ovac-PZO(111)) + 1/2 E(O2) - E(perfect-PZO(111)) (9)

where E(Ovac-PZO(111)) and E(perfect-PZO(111)) are the total energies of the defect PZO (111) surface and perfect PZO (111) surface, respectively. E(O2) is the total energy of free O2 molecules with triplet.

The adsorption energy of H2O molecule (Eads) is defined as

Eads = E(H2O-Ovac-PZO(111)) - E(H2O) - E(Ovac-PZO(111)) (10)

where E(H2O-Ovac-PZO(111)) and E(Ovac-PZO(111)) are the total energies of the defect PZO (111) surface with and without H2O molecule adsorption, respectively. E(H2O) is the total energy of free H2O molecules.

The Gibbs free energy is calculated by

G = E + ΔGDFT-cor (11)

where E represents the energy from DFT calculations, and ΔGDFT-cor denotes the free energy correction calculated using the VASP toolkit (vaspkit)61.

The desorption energy of oxygen molecules is calculated by

Edes = E(PZO(111)) + E(O2) - E(O2-PZO(111)) (12)

where E(PZO(111)) and E(O2-PZO(111)) represent the total energies of the PZO (111) surface without and with oxygen molecule adsorption, respectively. E(O2) represents the energy of the free oxygen molecule.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript introduces Pr₃ZrO₈ (PZO) as a promising redox material for two-step thermochemical water splitting, a sustainable technology for the co-production of hydrogen and oxygen. This work lies in PZO’s ability to operate effectively at intermediate temperatures—specifically, 900 °C for thermal reduction (oxygen release) and 400 °C for chemical oxidation (hydrogen evolution). Structurally, PZO adopts a face-centered cubic lattice, analogous to CeO₂, yet demonstrates a significantly higher oxygen off-stoichiometry, a critical parameter governing its redox reactivity. The claims are supported by variable-temperature neutron diffraction (VTND) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA).
1. While the manuscript offers some insights into the development of intermediate-temperature redox materials, several key issues must be addressed and experimentally validated to fully assess the significance of this work.
2. What are the maximum and minimum values of oxygen non-stoichiometry (δ) that PZO can accommodate without compromising its crystallographic stability? A precise understanding of δ boundaries under both oxidizing and reducing conditions is essential for evaluating and optimizing the redox performance of PZO. Currently, the lack of such data limits our ability to benchmark PZO against state-of-the-art redox materials and to optimize its operational parameters for improved energy efficiency.
3. Although the manuscript emphasizes oxygen non-stoichiometry, it overlooks the potential role of Pr and Zr cation vacancies in influencing redox behavior. These defects may significantly affect oxygen mobility and catalytic performance. A discussion and supporting data regarding cationic defect chemistry are needed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of PZO's redox mechanism.
4. Despite the detailed Rietveld refinement of VTND data—capturing temperature-dependent changes in lattice parameters, bonding, and oxygen vacancies—reciprocal space mapping (RSM) is crucial. RSM can reveal localized strain, defects, and phase transitions, which are indispensable for assessing the material’s thermal stability, defect dynamics, and catalytic performance under operational conditions. Unfortunately, such information is missing in this manuscript.
5. The current characterization strategy lacks sufficient insight into local atomic environments and defect structures. A thorough investigation using XAS would allow quantification of local lattice distortions and vacancies (oxygen, Pr, and Zr), enabling a direct correlation between atomic-scale structure and macroscopic redox properties. This is important for identifying active sites and understanding structural transformations during cycling.
6. The temperature profile employed during the VTND measurements must be clearly provided. In Figure 3, the change in lattice parameters at 300 °C suggests that the structure had not reached thermal equilibrium prior to the subsequent scan at 400 °C. To ensure meaningful analysis, neutron scans should be performed only after confirming structural stabilization at each temperature step.
7. As XPS is inherently semi-quantitative, it is not suitable for accurately benchmarking stoichiometry. Therefore, the use of a standard reference sample with a well-defined composition is essential for calibrating TGA data, which plays a central role in quantifying oxygen exchange. Moreover, TGA analysis must be preceded by rigorous pre-oxidation and proper calibration of the sample. Without these critical steps, the resulting data may lead to misinterpretations of the material’s true oxygen storage capacity and redox behaviour.

### Reviewer 2

Useful extension of examination of ceria based oxides for intermediate temperature thermochemical productions of oxygen and hydrogen that selects elements that render ceria more readily reducible like PrxCe1-xO2-y and ZrxCe1-xO2-y. While the authors reference some of this work, I would ask them to reference PrxCe1-xO2-y given the similarity to the system chosen in this study. That being said, this represents examination of an additional interesting and promising offshoot of the others offering lower temperature operation, albeit some dangers in going too far in reduction and generating second phases that may create sluggish reoxidation pathways.
My major problems with the manuscript are suspect conductivity data and incorrect defect/transport models. To begin with, the general trends of conductivity vs pO2 are not unreasonable. However the abrupt shift from an ~1/8th slope in the log/log plot at 500C and above to ~1/4 at 475C and below makes no sense. Defect equilibria do not undergo such step changes over such small steps in temperature. The authors need to investigate what caused such a dramatic change in pO2 dependence.
The other, even more serious issue is there analysis of the defect equilibria and its impact on electron transport. In lines 184 and 185, they suggest a small polaron hopping model for electron transport similar to that ealier reported for PrxCe1-xO2-y in which electrons can hop from occupied Pr3+ ions to nearby unoccupied Pr4+ ions (e.g S. R. Bishop, et al, Electrical Conductivity and Defect Equilibria of Pr0.1Ce0.9O2-δ, Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics 13, 10165-10173 (2011)). Here the authors introduce 3 oxidation states for Pr 2,3 & 4+. The small polaran model assumes only 2 oxidation states and there is no reason to assume that Pr2+ exists, particularly if the crystal structure remains fluorite. The defect model needs to be rethought and redone.

Line 180: states in text: Figure 5(a) indicates that PZO is a semiconductor, i.e. conductivity increases with T. Yes but so does ionic conductivity!
Line 190: Should be Pr3+ No evidence of Pr2+
In eq. 6 mixing up concentrations of defects [VO] with fractions of sites (cid:1). Not at all clear that Zr should be treated as an aliovalent element since fluorite structure is the reference.

## Paper

## Abstract

Two-step thermochemical cycles offer a clean route for hydrogen and oxygen production but are typically limited to high temperatures exceeding 1500 °C. Lowering operating temperatures would enable the use of alternative heat sources such as industrial waste heat. Here, we report Pr3ZrO8-δ as a new enabling material for efficient intermediate-temperature redox cycling, with thermal reduction at 900 °C in argon and steam oxidation at 400 °C. Pr3ZrO8-δ adopts a face-centered cubic structure similar to CeO2 but exhibits significantly greater oxygen deficiency, achieving average oxygen and hydrogen fluxes of 331.7 and 70.3 µmol·g-1, respectively, over ten cycles at 20% H2O. These values surpass those of leading CeO2-δ and perovskite oxides under comparable or more severe conditions. In-situ neutron and X-ray diffraction determine the phase stability boundaries of Pr3ZrO8-δ, while density functional theory identifies O-H bond cleavage as the rate-limiting step. These results establish Pr3ZrO8-δ as a promising material for intermediate-temperature thermochemical oxygen and hydrogen production.

---

## Introduction

The realization of a clean and sustainable energy future hinges on the availability of low-cost hydrogen on a large scale. The current benchmark technology for bulk H2 production, steam methane reforming (SMR) technology is cost effective and energy efficient but emits significant amounts of CO2 (~9 kg CO2 per kg H2 produced), which would impose a marked negative impact on the environment if allowed to release into the atmosphere without restriction1,2. While adding CO2 capture facilities to SMR plants is technically possible, it would considerably raise the cost of H2. Electrolytic production of H2 (green H2) from water is a clean technology, but it is still too expensive to be deployed at commercial scale. Similarly, the current commercial cryogenic distillation based bulk O2 production is also an energy intensive and costly process. Searching for clean, cost-effective, and scalable O2 and H2 production technologies is, therefore, of paramount importance to a sustainable clean energy future.

Solar-driven thermochemical (TC) approach stands out to be an appealing method for clean, scalable, and low-cost O2 and H2 production from water, using only solar heat as an energy source3–5. This approach leverages the entire solar spectrum for high temperature heat generation at desirable locations where the active material undergoes TC redox cycles for separate O2 and H2 productions6. Oxygen off-stoichiometric CeO2-δ is currently the benchmark TC material due to its reversible single-phase redox chemistry under the thermal and chemical cycling conditions7. The “two-step” thermal reduction and water splitting cycles can be represented by:

CeO2 = CeO2-δre + 0.5δre O2 ↑ (1)

CeO2-δre + (δre - δox)H2O = CeO2-δox + (δre - δox)H2 ↑ (2)

It is evident that the amount of oxygen released during the thermal reduction cycle is proportional to off-stoichiometry δre under a thermal reduction temperature (Ttr) and partial pressure of oxygen (pO2), whereas the hydrogen released during the steam splitting cycle is proportional to the difference between δre and oxygen off-stoichiometry δox under a steam splitting temperature (Twp) and pO2. Since CeO2 has a relatively low δre and δox, it must operate at a high Ttr (e.g., ~1500 °C) and Twp (e.g., ~1200 °C) to yield practically meaningful production rates of H2 and O2.

The strict requirement for high Ttr (heat demand) operation is undesirable for TC processes. This increases the solar energy demand and lowers the overall solar-to-fuel and solar-to-oxidant efficiencies. It also accelerates the sintering of redox materials, which causes reduction in active surface area and degradation in performance8–12. To reduce Ttr of reaction (1), one noticeable research effort is to remove O2 from the reactor during the cycle so that the equilibrium of reaction (1) can be shifted to the right. These methods include vacuuming10, chemical scavenging13, and oxygen transport membranes14. Challenges to implement these methods are the further-reduced solar-to-fuel (STF) efficiency (e.g., from ~5% to <1.73%) due to the low pumping efficiency (<1%) at low pressures (<10−5 atm)10,11 and increased system complexity and cost. Therefore, identification of new redox materials that can operate at lower Ttr is a preferred option to the development of commercially viable solar TC technologies.

Developing new redox active oxides (RAOs) with higher oxygen off-stoichiometry than CeO2-δ has been a focal area for the “two-step” TC research in recent decades. Given TCs’ harsh operating conditions15, RAOs need to (1) be chemically and thermally stable over a wide range of pO216; (2) exhibit large change in oxygen off-stoichiometry (Δδ) during the “two-step” cycles17; (3) show high mixed oxide-ion and electron conductivity18. Based on these criteria, off-stoichiometric oxides have attracted the most interests19. Representatives of this class of RAOs include transition-metal doped CeO211, iron aluminates20 and perovskites ABO3 (A=La, Ca, Sr, Ba, etc.; B=Mn, Fe, Co, etc.)20–25. While these materials exhibit greater δre over pure CeO2-δ, the overall TC cycling temperature window is still too high. Early studies have also considered volatile stoichiometric chemistries (e.g., ZnO/Zn and SnO2/SnO) for TC by leveraging the high entropy change of phase transformation during thermal reduction cycle26,27. However, one challenge for these volatile cycles is the difficulty of separating the reduced products from oxygen.

Here, we report a new RAO for intermediate temperature “two-step” TC production of O2 and H2. The new material has a composition of Pr3ZrO8-δ (PZO) with a high level of oxygen off-stoichiometry and face centered cubic (fcc) structure. We show that fcc-PZO substantially outperforms the benchmark CeO2-δ as well as other perovskites in δ and H2/O2 yields through TC cycle even under reduced temperatures and low steam concentrations, making it a promising class of RAO for new-generation reduced temperature TC processes driven by a variety of heat sources.

---

## Results

Initial XRD check
A room-temperature lab XRD was first performed to quickly check the crystal structure of the as-synthesized PZO. Figure 1 shows the pattern that can be well indexed into the fcc structure with a lattice parameter of 5.43 Å. Therefore, PZO can also be viewed as a fluorite structured composition of Pr0.75Zr0.25O2 after doping ZrO2 into PrO2 in a stoichiometric ratio of Pr:Zr = 3:1.

VTND analysis
To precisely examine the evolutions of crystal structure and crystallographic parameters of PZO with temperature and atmospheres, we employed VTND (Variable Temperature Neutron Diffraction). The VTND patterns in 2D and 3D contour style collected in the range of RT-900 °C in argon (relevant to TC condition) are shown in Fig. 2a, b. The real-time phase evolution can be clearly visualized from the intensity contour plots. The refined crystal structure is shown in Fig. 2c along with refinement data listed in Table S1 of the Supplementary Information (SI).

At room temperature, the diffraction patterns can be well refined into space group Fm3¯m (No. 225) with very low Bragg-intensity R values (Rp) and weight-profile R value (Rwp). In this fluorite structure, Pr/Zr and O occupies (0, 0, 0) and (1/4, 1/4, 1/4), respectively. More importantly, Zr shares Pr position with 25% occupancy without showing a long-range ordering, which suggests that the original Pr3ZrO8-δ can be viewed as Pr0.75Zr0.25O2-δ. It is also interesting to note that 91.5% of the O-site in PZO is occupied at RT, suggesting 8.5% oxygen vacancies (δo=0.17) and the as-synthesized PZO composition as Pr0.75Zr0.25O1.83 at RT.

With the same fcc structure, we also refined VTND patterns at other temperatures. The original refined patterns and refined structure are provided in Fig. S1 with data in Table S1. From these data, we can conclude that PZO retains its fcc structure from RT to 900 °C in argon with neither phase transition nor impurity detected, indicating thermal stability of PZO in argon up to 900 °C. Similar datasets collected in air and refinement performed are provided in Figs. S2–S3 and Table S2. As evident from these results, there is no phase change from RT to 900 °C in air either.

The refined lattice parameter, unit cell volume and bond length between Pr(Zr) and O as a function of T in air and argon are compared in Fig. 3. In air, lattice parameter a (Å), unit cell volume (Å3) and Pr(Zr)-O bond length (Å) increase with T as expected. In argon, a similar trend with T is observed. However, the lattice parameter, unit volume and Pr(Zr)-O bond length of PZO are all larger in argon than in air. These increases are obviously caused by the loss of lattice oxygen that weakens Pr(Zr)-O interactions and formation of large Pr3+28,29, allowing lattice to expand and Pr-O bond to elongate.

It is interesting to point out that the lattice parameter measured in air exhibits a small contraction with time at 300 °C, signaling that there might be a small change in lattice oxygen content. In comparison, the lattice parameter measured at 300 °C in argon exhibits a significant increase in the later stage of the 300 °C-holding period, further inferring a possible change in lattice oxygen content. Our later TGA and TC cycling results suggest that this is likely related to the dynamics of oxygen release. While the lattice parameter measured in air remains normal at higher temperatures, they exhibit slightly different behaviors in argon. The first is from 400 to 500 °C, where there is a significant change in lattice parameter, followed by a slower change from 500 to 600 °C. Another occurs at 800 °C, where the expected plateau is taken over by a slower increase. Again, these lattice parameter abnormalities signal that there are some subtle changes in the PZO’s lattice oxygen content (and Pr oxidation state) with T, particularly in atmospheres with low pO2, although there is no clear evidence of phase transformation from all VTND patterns shown. With the data available, we hypothesize that Fig. 3a is the result of change in oxygen stoichiometry accompanied by the corresponding change in Pr-oxidation state and elongation of Pr-O bond. Oxygen occupancy cannot be precisely determined to further understand these subtle changes due to the short-time-bin data collection during the T-ramping period.

Phase stability of fcc-PZO
The phase stability of fcc-PZO under the working conditions of TC processes is critically important to the stability of H2/O2 yields. To determine the phase stability, we exposed the as-synthesized fcc-PZO samples in different T and pO2, followed by quenching the samples from high temperatures and analyzing the phase composition by XRD. According to the identified phases, we construct the phase stability diagram in Fig. 4. The original XRD patterns can be found in Fig. S4 in the SI. The impurities identified are Pr3+ compounds: Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7. A general trend is that the higher the pO2, the higher the T that fcc-PZO is stable.

We also performed high-temperature XRD (HTXRD) in air (pO2 = 0.21 atm) and high vacuum (pO2 ~ 10−9 atm) from RT to 1100 °C as an independent verification. The original HTXRD patterns are shown in Fig. S5. Shown in diamond in Fig. 4 are the phases identified by HTXRD; they fall well within the phase regions constructed from ex-situ XRD data, indicating the accuracy of the phase diagram.

We also attempted to construct the phase stability diagram using hybrid DFT coupling spin-orbital interactions; the details about the approach are provided in the Experimental section. Figure S6 shows the calculated phase stability diagram of the PZO system using this method. With the consideration of temperature and configurational entropy, the calculations show that a stable PZO phase could be formed.

Oxygen off-stoichiometry vs. T and pO2
Oxygen off-stoichiometry (δ) is a key parameter determining the performance of RAO in TC cycles. A precise determination of δ as a function of T and pO2 is critically important to understand the performance of PZO for TC applications. Therefore, we selected both VTND and TGA methods to evaluate δ of PZO. The VTND-derived δ values were taken as the twice the fraction of the unoccupied O-sites obtained from refinement; Tables S1 and S2 list these values measured in both air and argon and air, respectively. At RT, δo = 0.17, which is the same as δo = 0.17 estimated by XPS and XAS based on the oxidation state of Pr; see Figs. S7 and S8 in the SI.

To confirm the VTND-derived δ, we also performed TGA measurements; the original weight loss curves are shown in Fig. S9, from which δ = δ(T) is derived using δo = 0.17 as the starting value. Figure 5a compares the two sets of δ in the formula of Pr0.75Zr0.25O2-δ. Note that VTND-data are only available in air and argon. The VTND-derived δ consistently exhibits a slightly higher value than its TGA-derived counterpart in both atmospheres. Within the experimental error, the two sets of δ-values agree with each other. Correspondingly, the oxidation state of Pr is also plotted against T in the second y-axis in Fig. 5a. As is shown, the average oxidation state of Pr decreases as T increases and pO2 decreases, implying that more Pr3+ is formed while the lattice oxygen is being lost. A plot of log δ vs. 1/T shown in Fig. 5b confirms that the loss of oxygen or the formation of oxygen vacancies is a thermally activated process following Arrhenius relationship with a very low activation energy of 0.02−0.03 eV, suggesting that the thermal oxygen release in PZO is a very facile process. An early study has also confirmed in CeO2-ZrO2 system that Zr4+ facilitates reducibility of pure CeO230. Our DFT calculations also confirm the low formation energy of oxygen vacancies in fcc-PZO even at oxygen-rich condition, see Figs. S10–S11 in the SI; details about the DFT method are provided in the Experimental Methods section.

A simple conversion of Pr-oxidation state shown in Fig. 5a into Pr3+ concentration ([Pr3+]) using charge neutrality indicates that there is ~75% Pr3+ present in the fcc-PZO under 900 oC and N2, see Fig. S12, which is in striking difference from pure PrO2; the latter turns into Pr2O3 or other lower oxidation state intermediates (PrnO2n-2) under this condition31. Therefore, it is reasonable to believe that Zr4+ stabilizes Pr4+, likely due to its fixed-valence substitution.

To compare with the benchmark CeO2-δ, we further plot δ-pO2-T of fcc-PZO in Fig. 6. A first glance indicates that fcc-PZO exhibits much higher δ than CeO2-δ, particularly at lower T range. To put this into perspective, δ at 900 °C in argon and in air are 0.27 and 0.24, respectively. For the benchmark CeO2-δ, it is in the order of 10−4 and 10−3 in air and argon, respectively19,32. The significant advantage of PZO in δre over CeO2-δ strongly suggests that PZO is a promising RAO for intermediate temperature TC processes.

Understanding electrical conductivity vs. T and pO2
Electrical conductivity is a crucial indicator of bulk diffusion of ions/electrons and charge transfer kinetics at the surface of PZO. The measured total electrical conductivity σ of PZO as a function of pO2 and T is shown in Fig. 7. The level of conductivity over the entire pO2 and T ranges studied is rather low (10−2 to 10−3 S/cm) but comparable to CeO2-δ at much higher temperatures and lower pO2. Collectively, Fig. 7 indicates that PZO is a semiconductor with a low activation energy Ea = 0.34−0.43 eV (Fig. 7b). At high pO2 range (>10-4 atm), Fig. 7a indicates that fcc-PZO displays a p-type conducting behavior. As pO2 decreases, σ first experiences a plateau, an indicative of dominance of ionic defects, then a weak n-type conducting behavior.

To interpret the conductivity behavior described above, we developed a simplified defect-chemistry model based on the “dilute solution” approximation; full derivations are provided in the Supplementary Information. Briefly, the model adopts the fluorite (fcc) lattice as the reference framework and assumes Pr4+ (Pr×Pr) as the base oxidation state. Under a given T and pO2, oxygen loss generates oxygen vacancy (V••O), Pr3+ (Pr'Pr) species as described by reaction (S1) in the SI.

At high pO2 (>10−3 atm), oxygen vacancies are oxidized to produce electron holes (reaction (S2)), giving rise to p-type conductivity. Conversely, at low pO2 (<10−7 atm), lattice oxygen (O×O) is removed (reaction (S3)), generating free electrons and yielding n-type conductivity. In the intermediate pO2 range (~10−7 to 10−3 atm), ionic defects (V••O and Pr'Pr) dominate, while electronic carriers remain minority species. Consequently, overall conductivity becomes less sensitive to pO2. We note that both oxygen vacancies and electrons are present in fcc-PZO at comparatively high concentrations; however, because electrons possess much higher mobility, the total conductivity is still dominated by electronic charge transport even within the intermediate pO2 regime. Therefore, fcc-PZO is deemed a mixed electronic and oxide-ion conductor.

The above defect-chemistry picture is consistent with prior band-structure studies on Pr oxides. These studies show that the partially filled Pr4+ 4f1 band resides near the Fermi level and strongly hybridizes with the O-2p valance band, leading PrO2-δ, including fcc-PZO, to exhibit narrow-band semiconducting behavior with a band gap ~0.5 eV associated with mixed Pr3+/Pr4+ valance state33. This prediction agrees with the measured activation energy of ~0.4 eV in Fig. 7b. In contrast, Pr3+ contains strongly localized 4f2 electrons, and Pr2O3 behaves as a Mott insulator with a significantly large band gap (3.5–4.5 eV) between the O-2p valance band and Pr-5d/4f conduction band34. Because Pr4+ species provide the electronic states that facilitate charge transport, the conductivity naturally decreases as the Pr4+ concentration diminishes with decreasing pO2. Notably, a substantial amount of Pr4+ - approximately 25% even under 900 oC and N2 condition - is observed in the fcc-PZO system (Fig. S12).

Thermochemical performance of PZO
To search for the best TC working conditions, we first performed single-cycle testing on fcc-PZO under different T-window (i.e., between Ttr and Tws) and H2O contents. Note that the high T-value within the T-window represents the temperature (Ttr) for thermal reduction cycle, whereas the low T-value is the temperature (Tws) for water splitting reaction cycle. Figure 8a shows the effect of T-window on H2 generation flux under a fixed 20% H2O-Ar; the corresponding set of O2 flux is given in Fig. S14a. It is evident that there is a significant gain in H2 flux from 1100 to 900 °C window to 1100–500 °C window, but no significant gain is observed for 1100–400 °C window. On the other hand, cycling within 900–400 °C produces similar H2 flux as 1100–900 °C cycling. However, our phase diagram (Fig. 4) as well as the following post-test analysis indicate that exposure of fcc-PZO to argon above 1000 °C leads to its decomposition to Pr2O3. Therefore, 900–400 °C is selected as the T-window for TC cycling of fcc-PZO. On the other hand, the effect of H2O on H2 flux is shown in Fig. 8b along with the corresponding O2 flux shown in Fig. S14b, suggesting that H2O contents higher than 20% do not increase H2 flux significantly within the 400–900 °C window.

These selection of the above cycling conditions, i.e., 900–400 °C and 20% H2O is further supported by the post-test analysis. Figure 8c shows that at Ttr ≥ 1000 °C, fcc-PZO partially decomposes into Pr2O3, which is an oxide-ion and electron insulator and detrimental to TC performance. Upon exposure to 20% H2O for 4 h at 400 °C in the following oxidation cycle, Fig. 8d shows that the fcc-PZO exposed to Ar at Ttr ≤ 900 °C remains unchanged in phase compositions (red patterns). In contrast, for fcc-PZO exposed to 1000 °C in Ar (blue patterns), it is interesting to observe that the Pr2O3 secondary phase is reversed to the original fcc phase after H2O oxidation cycle, demonstrating the reversibility. A partial conversion of Pr2O3 impurity to Pr6O11 is also observed after H2O oxidation of fcc-PZO that was exposed to 1100 °C in argon (green patterns). These results suggest that the reoxidation of Pr2O3 into Pr6O11 or fcc-PZO is thermodynamically feasible but could be kinetically limited. Based on the above results, we, therefore, select 900 °C for thermal reduction cycles in argon and 400 °C for water splitting cycles in 20% H2O.

The original profiles of T, O2 and H2 concentrations collected under this condition over 10 consecutive TC cycles are shown in Fig. 9a, by which the O2/H2 fluxes are converted and plotted against cycle number in Fig. 9b. In general, this level of intermediate-temperature performance is better than most reported in the literature even under higher temperatures, see Table S3 for comparison, demonstrating the potential of fcc-PZO for reduced temperature TC applications. Note that fcc-PZO represents a fundamentally distinct material class from the extensively studied CeO2-ZrO2 solid solution systems; the latter has consistently underperformed the benchmark CeO2-δ 10,19,35–38. Unlike CeO2-ZrO2 solid solutions, fcc-PZO functions more like a compound, akin to CeO2. However, excessive reduction of Pr4+ to Pr3+ could lead to the undesirable formation of Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7, see phase diagram Fig. 4. A key role of Zr in the system is stabilization of the Pr4+/Pr3+ redox couple within the fcc structure by limiting excessive oxygen release, thereby alleviating the formation of the unwanted Pr2O3 and Pr2Zr2O7 impurity phases. Compared to another similar system Ce0.8Pr0.2O2-δ (CPO, the “sweet-spot” composition in the CeO2-Pr2O3 series), where Pr3+ substitution is employed to stabilize oxygen vacancies and lower the reduction enthalpy39–42, fcc-PZO has a clear advantage in δ. For example, the Pr-rich fcc-PZO exhibits δ = 0.20–0.25 in air over 600–900 °C, vs. 0.02–0.08 for CPO39, largely due to suppressed Pr4+ to Pr3+ reduction by Zr4+.

It is evident from Fig. 9b that there is more O2 than H2 produced in each cycle, i.e., 331.7 µmol/g for O2 flux vs. 70.3 µmol/g for H2 flux (averaged from the 10 cycles), which significantly deviates from the theoretical ratio of H2/O2 = 2/1. The slow kinetics for water splitting reaction at lower temperature as evidenced by the longer cycle time than thermal reduction cycle, i.e., 2 h vs. 1 h, is likely the reason. In other words, it may take a much longer time for the water splitting cycle to occupy all available oxygen vacancies and reach the theoretical H2 flux. Accumulation of unfilled oxygen vacancies due to incomplete oxidation cycle could lead to a gradual loss of oxygen and hydrogen fluxes during the subsequent reduction cycle, resulting in the degradation shown in Fig. 9b.

It is worth noting that the steam utilization in this laboratory testing is very low, which leads to very low H2/H2O ratio during the water splitting cycle. One concern is whether fcc-PZO is still stable at lower pO2 (higher H2/H2O ratio). To test this possibility, we performed a separate study in which we directly expose fcc-PZO to 4% H2-Ar for 2 h at 900 °C. The XRD pattern of the tested sample is shown in Fig. S15, where the original fcc-PZO peaks remain without any detectable impurity phases. The XRD peaks are slightly shifted to the left, implying increased oxygen off-stoichiometry. Therefore, this study at least confirms that fcc-PZO is stable at 900 °C up to 4% H2.

To facilitate the understanding of the observed degradation, we also examined the morphology of the tested fcc-PZO by SEM and compared it with the one before testing in Fig. S16. No significant change in fcc-PZO morphology can be detected after cycling, which is not surprising given the low temperature operation. Therefore, the degradation is likely due to the slow water splitting kinetics that causes the chain-reaction reducing the amount of available oxygen vacancies to sustain the thermochemical cycling.

Understanding the rate limiting step of the steam splitting cycle
To facilitate the understanding of the underlying reasons for the lower-than-anticipated H2 production in the water splitting cycle and identification of the rate limiting step (RLS), we conducted an analysis of the Gibbs free energy associated with the elementary steps using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. We first constructed three low index surfaces of fcc-PZO, namely, PZO (100), PZO (110), and PZO (111) from the optimized structure of the PZO bulk, as illustrated in Fig. S17. In accordance with the definition of surface energy, the calculated surface energies for PZO (100), PZO (110), and PZO (111) are 2.02, 0.51, and 0.24 J/m2, respectively. Generally, a thermodynamically stable crystal face is characterized by lower surface energy, indicating that the PZO (111) surface is the most stable surface. Consequently, we selected the PZO (111) surface for further DFT analysis. Figure S18 illustrates the construction process of the PZO (111) surface, including the optimized structure of the PZO unit cell, top and side views of the cleaved PZO (111) unit cell, and a 2x1x1 PZO (111) supercell.

The proposed elementary steps occurring on the surface of PZO (111) are as follows: (1) the formation of an oxygen-vacancy site (Ovac); (2) the adsorption of H2O onto an Ovac; (3) the splitting of H2O into two intermediate species (OH*); (4) the breakage of the OH bonds; and (5) the evolution of H2 molecule. Figure 10 illustrates both the top and side views of the reaction pathway along with the structural parameters, as well as the corresponding Gibbs free energy profiles for the H2O splitting process over the PZO (111) surface. Initially, an oxygen vacancy (Ovac) is generated by the release of one lattice oxygen from the pristine PZO (111) surface, which has an oxygen vacancy formation energy of -0.95 eV, see step b. Subsequently, an H2O molecule is adsorbed above the Ovac site, exhibiting an adsorption energy of −0.66 eV, see step c. It is noteworthy from Fig. 10b that, with the formation of the oxygen vacancy and the adsorption of the H2O molecule, the O1 atom in the subsurface gradually moves upward toward the surface. The distances between the O1 atom and the surface for steps a, b, and c are measured at 1.38 Å, 0.63 Å, and 0.10 Å, respectively. As the H atom (labeled as H2) approaches the adjacent O1 atom, a new H2-O1 bond is formed, resulting in its bond length from 1.44 to 1.02 Å. Concurrently, the H2-O3 bond within the H2O molecule breaks, leading to an elongation of its bond length from 1.07 to 1.66 Å. This sequence of events in the dissociation of H2O molecules requires a free energy change of −0.05 eV, forming two isolated OH* intermediates adsorbed on the surface. At step d, the dissociation of the H2O is complete. Subsequently, the two OH bonds, i.e., H2-O1 and H1-O3, are cleaved successively, with the corresponding Gibbs free energies being 0.60 eV and 1.67 eV, respectively. The high energy for H1-O3 cleavage indicates that this step is the RLS toward completing H2 evolution process. The reaction elementary steps and process energies are summarized in Table S4.

We observe that the oxygen vacancy formation energy in Table S4 is negative, implying that a lattice oxygen atom in the PZO (111) surface can be released spontaneously. Consequently, we conducted a further evaluation of the surface’s propensity for oxygen release at higher concentrations of oxygen vacancies. As illustrated in Fig. S19, the formation energies for the first and second oxygen vacancies are −0.95 eV and −0.25 eV, respectively. Moreover, the formation of oxygen vacancies facilitates the migration of subsurface oxygen atoms to the surface. These values indicate that the PZO (111) surface exhibits a strong tendency to release oxygen. Additionally, as illustrated in Fig. 9b, upon the completion of a H2O splitting cycle, we observe that the O1 atom in the subsurface migrates to the surface and forms oxygen molecule with O3, exhibiting an O1-O3 bond length of 1.29 Å. To further evaluate the oxygen release capacity of the PZO (111) surface, we calculated the desorption of this oxygen molecule. The results shown in Fig. S20 indicate a desorption energy of 0.26 eV, again suggesting that the PZO (111) surface can readily release oxygen. Overall, our computational results align well with experimental observations, i.e., the water splitting cycle is the RLS for PZO-based intermediate temperature TC processes, while thermal oxygen release cycle is facile. We are currently working to computationally identify effective surface catalysts that can promote O-H cleavage, followed by testing these catalysts in TC reactor.

In summary, we have demonstrated that PZO crystallizes in a face centered cubic (fcc) structure analogous to CeO2-δ yet exhibits significantly higher oxygen off-stoichiometry (δ), enabling hydrogen generation at lower temperatures. Under thermal reduction in argon at 900 °C, the 10-cycle averaged oxygen flux reaches 331.7 µmol g−1, while hydrogen production achieves 70.3 µmol g−1 at 400 °C with 20% H2O-performance that surpasses both benchmark CeO2-δ and most perovskite oxides under development. A comprehensive investigation combining in situ neutron diffraction, in situ XRD, and ex situ XRD has established the phase stability diagram of the fcc-PZO system, delineating its redox boundaries for thermochemical applications. Supported by experimental validation and hybrid DFT calculations including spin-orbit coupling interactions, a simplified defect chemistry model has been developed that integrates ionic (oxygen vacancies) and electronic (free electrons and holes) defects, providing key insights into charge-carrier transport mechanisms in fcc-PZO.

A remaining challenge for the practical deployment of fcc-PZO in intermediate-temperature TC processes lies in the kinetics of the steam-splitting reaction. Accelerating this step will be critical for realizing the full potential of fcc-PZO. Strategies such as applying surface catalysts or enhancing mixed oxide-ionic and electronic conductivity offer promising pathways to address this limitation. Preliminary DFT calculations indicate that the rate-limiting step (RLS) is the cleavage of the O-H bond on the PZO (111) surface. Overall, this study identifies PZO as a promising redox-active oxide (RAO) for low-temperature thermochemical hydrogen production, operable with a wide range of heat sources.
